# Solvable models and decoherence-driven transitions {#sec-decoherence}

We now build a mixed-state transition from a preparation protocol simple enough to solve. Start with an unentangled paramagnet, apply random nearest-neighbor pair errors, and discard the error record. Total symmetry charge stays fixed, ordinary order never develops, but nonlinear correlations can become long-ranged. The model connects SW-SSB to classical disorder, decoding thresholds, and the distinction between intrinsic and Rényi-weighted transitions [@lee2023; @chen2024separability; @lessa2025].

The derivation has three complementary representations. The error representation gives exact probabilities on a graph. On a chain it produces closed-form correlators. In two dimensions, its cycle redundancy becomes a random-bond Ising model. A second calculation in the $Z$ basis gives the clean Ising model governing Rényi-2. Deriving both makes the inequivalence of the diagnostics concrete.

## The pair-error channel on a graph

Let a connected graph have $N$ vertices and $E$ edges, with a qubit at each vertex. Initialize

$$
\rho_0=|+\rangle\langle+|^{\otimes N}.
$$

On each edge $e=(ij)$ apply independently

$$
\mathcal E_{p,e}(\rho)=(1-p)\rho+pZ_iZ_j\rho Z_iZ_j,
\qquad0\leq p\leq\tfrac12.
$$ {#eq-pair-error-channel}

All these superoperators commute. The edge gates can be scheduled in a bounded number of layers on a bounded-degree lattice. The output $\rho_p=\prod_e\mathcal E_{p,e}(\rho_0)$ is therefore generated by a strongly symmetric finite-depth channel: each Kraus operator commutes with $U=\prod_iX_i$.

Let $s_e\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether the error on edge $e$ occurred. Its probability is

$$
w_p(s)=\prod_ep^{s_e}(1-p)^{1-s_e}.
$$

The error product flips the $X$ eigenvalue at each endpoint of an occupied edge. Define a vertex charge bit

$$
n_i=(\partial s)_i=\sum_{e\ni i}s_e\pmod2.
$$ {#eq-error-boundary}

Here $\partial$ is the graph incidence map over the two-element field. Every edge has two endpoints, so $\sum_in_i=0$ modulo two. The output is diagonal in the $X$ basis:

$$
\rho_p=\sum_{n:\sum_i n_i=0}P_p(n)|n\rangle_X\langle n|,
\quad
P_p(n)=\sum_{s:\partial s=n}w_p(s).
$$ {#eq-syndrome-distribution}

The word *syndrome* anticipates error correction: $n$ records error endpoints but forgets which path connected them. Different edge strings with the same boundary differ by cycles.

For $i\ne j$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_pZ_iZ_j)=0$, because $Z_iZ_j$ has no diagonal matrix elements in this basis. In fact, no conventional long-range charged order is generated. All states have exact even total parity. The interesting structure is entirely in the nonlinear comparison between the probability distribution and its charge-shifted version.

At $p=0$, only $n=0$ occurs and the state is pure. At $p=1/2$, all edge strings are equally likely. The incidence map of a connected graph has rank $N-1$, so each even $n$ has $2^{E-N+1}$ preimages. Therefore

$$
P_{1/2}(n)=2^{-(N-1)},\qquad
\rho_{1/2}=\frac{I+U}{2^N}.
$$ {#eq-pair-error-endpoint}

The protocol interpolates between the pure paramagnet and the canonical parity ensemble without changing its total charge.

## Exact fidelity as a classical overlap

Let $\delta^{ij}$ denote the vertex bit string with ones at $i,j$ only. Conjugation by $A=Z_iZ_j$ permutes charge configurations:

$$
A\rho_pA=\sum_nP_p(n\oplus\delta^{ij})|n\rangle_X\langle n|.
$$

The two matrices commute. Hence

$$
F_Z(i,j)=R_1(i,j)=\sum_n\sqrt{P_p(n)P_p(n\oplus\delta^{ij})},
$$ {#eq-pair-error-fidelity}

and

$$
R_2(i,j)=\frac{\sum_nP_p(n)P_p(n\oplus\delta^{ij})}
{\sum_nP_p(n)^2}.
$$ {#eq-pair-error-r2}

These expressions contain no replica continuation. They are exact finite-size formulas and provide a direct numerical route: enumerate edge strings, accumulate probabilities by their boundaries, and shift the two endpoint bits.

One should sum probabilities for all indistinguishable error strings *before* taking square roots. Averaging the overlap for each error trajectory instead would keep an error record that the physical mixed state has discarded and would compute a different quantity.

## One-dimensional open chain: full solution

On a tree, the boundary $n$ uniquely determines the edge string $s$ subject to even total charge. There are no nontrivial cycles. On an open chain, toggling endpoint charges at $i,j$ therefore toggles exactly the $r=|i-j|$ bonds on the unique connecting path $\gamma$:

$$
s\longmapsto s\oplus\gamma.
$$

Use @eq-pair-error-fidelity and factor the sum edge by edge. Off the path, the contribution is $p+(1-p)=1$. On each path edge,

$$
\sum_{s_e=0,1}\sqrt{w_p(s_e)w_p(1-s_e)}=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}.
$$

Thus

$$
F_Z(r)=R_1(r)=\bigl[2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\bigr]^r.
$$ {#eq-chain-fidelity}

The same factorization gives the purity and Rényi-2 numerator:

$$
\operatorname{Tr}\rho_p^2=[p^2+(1-p)^2]^{N-1},
$$

$$
R_2(r)=\left[\frac{2p(1-p)}{p^2+(1-p)^2}\right]^r.
$$ {#eq-chain-r2}

Both have a finite correlation length for every $p<1/2$, with

$$
\xi_F^{-1}=-\ln[2\sqrt{p(1-p)}],\qquad
\xi_2^{-1}=-\ln\frac{2p(1-p)}{p^2+(1-p)^2}.
$$ {#eq-chain-lengths}

Writing $p=1/2-\epsilon$ gives $\xi_F^{-1}=2\epsilon^2+O(\epsilon^4)$ and $\xi_2^{-1}=8\epsilon^2+O(\epsilon^4)$. Their common endpoint transition has different approach scales. At $p=1/2$ both correlators equal one at every separation. There is no finite-noise-strength global SW-SSB transition on this nearest-neighbor open chain; order is reached only at complete dephasing.

The chain result also checks every normalization. At $p=0$ the state is pure and both correlators vanish for $r>0$. At $p=1/2$ the purity is $2^{-(N-1)}$ and the state is uniform on the even sector. For $r=0$ the insertion is identity and the correlators are one.

### A controlled local-fidelity calculation

The same chain also lets us test the 2026 local definition without guessing whether a finite-region value has saturated. Take an interval $R=[a,b]$ deep inside a much longer chain and a site $x\in R$. A reduced charge configuration on $R$ depends on the $m+1$ independent error bits $s_{a-1},\ldots,s_b$, where $m=b-a+1$. The two boundary-crossing bonds matter because charge can enter the interval from its complement.

For given charges $n_a,\ldots,n_b$, these $m+1$ bits have two possible values: a string $s$ and its bitwise complement $\bar s$. Their probabilities add:

$$
P_R(n)=w_p(s)+w_p(\bar s).
$$

Flipping only $n_x$ is represented by toggling the left path of $\ell_L=x-a+1$ bonds from $x$ to the exterior. Toggling the right path of $\ell_R=b-x+1$ bonds gives the same reduced charge change. The two paths are complementary within these $m+1$ bits. Put $b_p=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}$. The reduced-state one-point fidelity obeys the useful exact bounds

$$
\max\{b_p^{\ell_L},b_p^{\ell_R}\}
\leq F(\rho_R,Z_x\rho_RZ_x)
\leq \min\{1,b_p^{\ell_L}+b_p^{\ell_R}\}.
$$ {#eq-chain-local-fidelity-bounds}

To obtain the lower bound, retain the individual error bits as a classical auxiliary variable. Their distribution and the distribution shifted by the left path have overlap $b_p^{\ell_L}$, by the same edgewise calculation as @eq-chain-fidelity. Forgetting the error bits and retaining only the reduced charges is a stochastic channel, so fidelity cannot decrease. Repeat with the right path and take the better bound.

For the upper bound, sum over one representative from each pair $s,\bar s$ and use

$$
\sqrt{(u+v)(u'+v')}
\leq\sqrt{uu'}+\sqrt{uv'}+\sqrt{vu'}+\sqrt{vv'}.
$$

Here $u=w(s)$, $v=w(\bar s)$, and the primed weights use the left-path shift. Two terms reconstruct the full edge-string overlap for that left shift; the other two reconstruct the overlap for the complementary right shift. Their sums are respectively $b_p^{\ell_L}$ and $b_p^{\ell_R}$. Normalized fidelity is also at most one, completing @eq-chain-local-fidelity-bounds.

For a central probe with $\ell_L=\ell_R=\ell$, the local fidelity lies between $b_p^\ell$ and $2b_p^\ell$. It consequently vanishes as the probe moves far from the boundary for every $p<1/2$. At $p=1/2$, the reduced state is maximally mixed and its local fidelity equals one. Thus both the local and global definitions locate the same endpoint in this particular nearest-neighbor chain, despite their inequivalence in general.

This calculation illustrates a productive numerical strategy. A positive small-region fidelity is not sufficient evidence for order, but an analytic upper bound decaying to zero certifies absence of local order. Conversely, a volume-independent positive lower bound certifies its presence. Here both bounds are available from the two alternative paths by which a local charge can communicate with the boundary. The boundary distance, rather than only the number of sites, is the physically relevant scale.

### Time and the order of limits

The Lindblad generator $\mathcal L_e(\rho)=\gamma(Z_iZ_j\rho Z_iZ_j-\rho)$ produces

$$
p(t)=\frac{1-e^{-2\gamma t}}2.
$$

Inserting this into @eq-chain-fidelity gives $F(r,t)=[\sqrt{1-e^{-4\gamma t}}]^r$. At large time, $\xi_F\simeq2e^{4\gamma t}$. For every finite time, the infinite-distance correlator still vanishes; at fixed distance it approaches one as $t\to\infty$. The limits do not commute. This discrete-symmetry model should not be confused with a $U(1)$ diffusive model, whose finite-time length scales can grow very differently.

### What changes on a ring?

On a ring, $s$ and its complement $s\oplus\mathbf1$ have the same boundary. Therefore $P(n)$ sums their two probabilities. A two-point charge shift can use either arc of the ring. The open-chain formula is recovered in the thermodynamic bulk limit with $r$ fixed or much smaller than the ring circumference, but it is not the exact finite-ring formula at arbitrary $r$. This is a useful warning: global cycles and boundary conditions matter for nonlinear state overlaps.

## Two dimensions: cycles become dual spins

On a planar square lattice, choose one error string $s^0$ with boundary $n$. Every other solution is $s=s^0\oplus\ell$, where $\ell$ is a closed loop configuration. Represent loops as domain walls of Ising variables $t_p=\pm1$ on dual plaquettes, including an exterior plaquette with fixed spin for an open planar sample. If edge $e$ separates dual plaquettes $p,q$,

$$
(-1)^{s_e}=\eta_e t_pt_q,\qquad \eta_e=(-1)^{s_e^0}.
$$

An individual edge probability can be written as

$$
p^{s_e}(1-p)^{1-s_e}
=\sqrt{p(1-p)}\exp[K(-1)^{s_e}],
\quad e^{-2K}=\frac p{1-p}.
$$

Substitute this in @eq-syndrome-distribution:

$$
P_p(n)=[p(1-p)]^{E/2}
\sum_{\{t_p\}}\exp\left[K\sum_{e=(pq)}\eta_et_pt_q\right].
$$ {#eq-rbim-syndrome-map}

The sum is the partition function of a random-bond Ising model on the dual lattice. The disorder signs encode the frustration required by the charge endpoints. Changing the representative $s^0$ by a loop is a dual gauge transformation and leaves this partition function unchanged. On a torus, one must additionally sum over noncontractible loop sectors; choosing only plaquette domain walls would omit them.

The disorder strength and coupling obey $\Pr(\eta_e=-1)=p$ and $e^{-2K}=p/(1-p)$ when the representative is sampled from the actual error distribution. This relation is the **Nishimori line** [@nishimori1980; @dennis2002]. It ties the inference model's assumed noise probabilities to those that generated the data.

To see the disorder average precisely, note that for any function $g$ of a syndrome,

$$
\sum_nP_p(n)g(n)=\sum_sw_p(s)g(\partial s).
$$

The right side permits choosing the actual sampled string as representative, giving independent random bonds. There is no need to guess a probability distribution for frustrations separately.

## Charge transfer as a disorder defect

Choose a path $\gamma$ from $i$ to $j$. The representative $s^0\oplus\gamma$ has boundary $n\oplus\delta^{ij}$. In the dual Ising partition function this reverses the signs of the bonds crossing the path. The ratio

$$
\frac{P_p(n\oplus\delta^{ij})}{P_p(n)}
=\frac{Z_{\eta\oplus\gamma}}{Z_\eta}
=e^{-\Delta\mathcal F_{ij}(\eta)}
$$ {#eq-defect-free-energy}

defines a dimensionless defect free-energy cost. Its path dependence is removable by dual gauge transformations, up to global topology. The endpoints are disorder-operator insertions. Consequently,

$$
F_Z(i,j)=R_1(i,j)=
\mathbb E_{\eta,\mathrm{Nishimori}}
\left[e^{-\Delta\mathcal F_{ij}(\eta)/2}\right].
$$ {#eq-fidelity-nishimori-moment}

This is a half-moment of a partition-function ratio, not the ordinary disorder-averaged spin correlation and not simply the exponential of a typical free energy.

At weak noise the dual RBIM is ferromagnetically ordered. A long defect line costs free energy proportional to its length, and the fidelity decays. At stronger noise the dual model is disordered, defect endpoints have a finite asymptotic cost, and fidelity becomes long-ranged. Thus *disorder* of the dual Ising model corresponds to SW-SSB *order* of the original density matrix.

### Why a typical-defect argument is insufficient

Jensen's inequality gives

$$
F_Z(i,j)\geq\exp[-\mathbb E\Delta\mathcal F_{ij}/2].
$$

A bounded mean defect cost is therefore sufficient for a nonzero lower bound. An extensive positive mean does not, by itself, prove exponential decay: rare disorder samples can dominate an exponential moment. In fact, normalization gives the exact identity

$$
\mathbb E[e^{-\Delta\mathcal F_{ij}}]
=\sum_nP_p(n)\frac{P_p(n\oplus\delta^{ij})}{P_p(n)}=1
$$ {#eq-defect-normalization-identity}

for $0<p<1/2$. The first moment stays one even where the half-moment decays. This explicitly demonstrates the importance of the full defect-cost distribution. The identification of the critical point and exponents uses the established Nishimori statistical mechanics and direct numerical work, beyond the elementary typical-domain-wall argument [@lessa2025; @wangreview2026].

For the nearest-neighbor square-lattice model the intrinsic transition occurs at approximately

$$
p_c\simeq0.109.
$$ {#eq-nishimori-threshold}

This is a numerical estimate, not a closed-form exact result. At criticality the root-fidelity/Rényi-1 correlator decays algebraically; the review reports numerical estimates around $\eta\simeq0.16$–$0.17$ for this half-moment and correlation-length exponents around $\nu\simeq1.3$–$1.5$. These ranges reflect numerical determinations and conventions, not rigorous universal bounds. The equality $F=R_1$ is exact in this commuting model.

## Rényi-2 maps to a clean Ising model

The clean mapping is most transparent in the $Z$ basis. Label configurations by $z_i=\pm1$. The initial density matrix has every entry equal to $2^{-N}$. Conjugation by an edge error multiplies the entry $(z,z')$ by $(z_iz_j)(z_i'z_j')$. Thus

$$
\rho_p(z,z')=2^{-N}\prod_{e=(ij)}
\left[(1-p)+p\tau_i\tau_j\right],\qquad
\tau_i=z_iz_i'.
$$ {#eq-z-basis-density-matrix}

Put $a=1-2p>0$. The bracket equals one for $\tau_i\tau_j=+1$ and $a$ for $-1$, so it is $\sqrt a\,e^{K_0\tau_i\tau_j}$ with $e^{-2K_0}=a$. Squaring the density-matrix entries and summing gives

$$
\operatorname{Tr}\rho_p^2
=2^{-N}a^E\sum_{\{\tau\}}
e^{K_2\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\tau_i\tau_j},
\qquad K_2=2K_0=-\ln(1-2p).
$$ {#eq-purity-clean-ising}

The factor $2^{-N}$ follows because each relative configuration $\tau$ has $2^N$ pairs $(z,z')$. For the numerator with $A=Z_xZ_y$, an extra factor $z_xz_yz_x'z_y'=\tau_x\tau_y$ appears. Therefore

$$
R_2(x,y)=\langle\tau_x\tau_y\rangle_{\mathrm{clean\ Ising},K_2}.
$$ {#eq-r2-clean-ising}

On the infinite square lattice, the clean Ising critical coupling is $K_c=\frac12\ln(1+\sqrt2)$. Solving $K_2(p_c^{(2)})=K_c$ gives

$$
p_c^{(2)}=\frac{1-\sqrt{\sqrt2-1}}2\simeq0.178203.
$$ {#eq-r2-threshold}

This threshold follows exactly from the clean model's critical point. At it $R_2(r)\sim r^{-1/4}$ and $\xi_2\sim|p-p_c^{(2)}|^{-1}$. It lies well inside the fidelity-ordered regime $p>p_c$. Thus the two-copy correlator has an additional critical singularity without defining an additional fidelity-order boundary.

| Channel parameter | Fidelity and Rényi-1 | Rényi-2 | Ordinary charged correlator |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0\leq p<p_c$ | Short-ranged | Short-ranged | Zero for separated $Z$ insertions |
| $p_c<p<p_c^{(2)}$ | Long-ranged | Short-ranged | Zero |
| $p_c^{(2)}<p\leq1/2$ | Long-ranged | Long-ranged | Zero |

This table excludes the critical points themselves, where the relevant correlator is algebraic rather than a nonzero asymptotic constant.

## Recoverability and the physical phase boundary

If $p_1<p_2<1/2$, applying additional pair dephasing of strength

$$
q=\frac{p_2-p_1}{1-2p_1}
$$ {#eq-channel-composition-noise}

takes $\rho_{p_1}$ to $\rho_{p_2}$. This follows from $1-2p_2=(1-2q)(1-2p_1)$. The nontrivial question is whether a strongly symmetric local channel can reverse that change on this family.

@lessa2025 constructs recovery using local Petz maps and the finite correlation scale of the associated RBIM away from its transition. States on the same side of the Nishimori transition can be connected in both directions with controlled shallow, logarithmic-scale constructions. Crossing the intrinsic boundary in the restoring direction is obstructed by fidelity stability. Crossing $p_c^{(2)}$ while remaining above $p_c$ does not obstruct that recovery. The Rényi-2 order can therefore disappear under a suitable strongly symmetric recovery channel even though fidelity order remains.

There is a subtle information-theoretic point. The SW-SSB phase can have a nonzero CMI plateau due to fixed global parity. Recovery of a strongly symmetric local deformation need not erase that plateau. The relevant sufficient condition is exponential smallness of the **CMI loss**

$$
\Delta I=I(A:C|B)_{\rho_{\mathrm{initial}}}
-I(A:C|B)_{\rho_{\mathrm{after\ local\ channel}}},
$$ {#eq-cmi-loss-recovery}

as the buffer grows, rather than exponential smallness of CMI itself. A charge-preserving deformation leaves the global constraint in place, and the common plateau cancels in $\Delta I$. Strong-symmetry-breaking erasure of one site does destroy it and cannot be repaired locally. These are different operations, fully consistent with the irrecoverability theorem.

The recovery derivation uses the statistical model's finite correlation length and control of boundary free energies, including intermediate spatially inhomogeneous states. It should not be promoted into a theorem that every arbitrary noisy family with one nonzero fidelity correlator has exactly two phases. The solvable model provides a well-supported instance of the more general framework.

## Beyond the Pauli model

Several deformations are scientifically distinct. Changing the initial state introduces correlations and possibly SPT order. Changing graph geometry or adding long-range pair channels changes the effective statistical mechanics. Replacing $Z_iZ_j$ by a continuous phase rotation changes the noise while preserving total parity. Adding single-site $Z_i$ errors explicitly removes strong symmetry and rounds or changes the problem.

For example, consider $(1-p)\rho+pe^{i\theta Z_iZ_j}\rho e^{-i\theta Z_iZ_j}$. Its off-diagonal weights involve $b=|1-p+pe^{2i\theta}|$. Replica calculations show the same relative-domain-wall structure as the Pauli channel, with a modified tension. @lessa2025 argues for Nishimori-type universality under suitable continuation assumptions. The Pauli mapping above is exact; the general non-Pauli universality conclusion uses replica reasoning and is accordingly less rigorous. Preserving that distinction prevents a useful physical conjecture from being mistaken for an unrestricted theorem.

The next chapters explain why the same error-endpoint probabilities govern quantum memory, how gauging promotes charge transport to string operators, and why different logical sectors can survive different amounts of decoherence.

## Exercises and worked solutions

### Exercise: the tree generalization

Derive the fidelity correlator on an arbitrary finite tree with nonuniform edge error probabilities $p_e$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The incidence map on a tree is a bijection from edge strings to even vertex syndromes. The unique path $\gamma_{ij}$ toggles the charge endpoints. Edgewise summation therefore yields $F_Z(i,j)=R_1(i,j)=\prod_{e\in\gamma_{ij}}2\sqrt{p_e(1-p_e)}$. Nonuniformity changes the accumulated tension, while branching alone does not create the cycle redundancy responsible for the two-dimensional planar mapping.
:::

### Exercise: derive the clean threshold

Starting from @eq-z-basis-density-matrix, explain why the coupling for Rényi-2 is $-\ln(1-2p)$ rather than $-\tfrac12\ln(1-2p)$, and solve for the square-lattice critical $p$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
An individual matrix element contains $e^{K_0\sum\tau_i\tau_j}$ with $K_0=-\frac12\ln(1-2p)$. The purity multiplies two matrix elements, doubling the coupling. Thus $K_2=2K_0$. Setting it equal to $K_c=\frac12\ln(1+\sqrt2)$ gives $1-2p=e^{-K_c}=\sqrt{\sqrt2-1}$ and @eq-r2-threshold. Forgetting the square would give the wrong threshold.
:::

### Exercise: a misleading disorder average

Why does @eq-defect-normalization-identity not force the half-moment fidelity to stay nonzero at large distance?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $X=e^{-\Delta\mathcal F}\geq0$. Knowing $\mathbb EX=1$ gives only $\mathbb E\sqrt X\leq1$ by concavity. For a simple example, let $X=M$ with probability $1/M$ and zero otherwise. Then $\mathbb EX=1$ but $\mathbb E\sqrt X=M^{-1/2}\to0$. Rare large likelihood ratios can preserve the first moment while the overlap measured by the half-moment vanishes.
:::

### Exercise: composition is not inversion

Can the additional-noise formula @eq-channel-composition-noise be used with $p_2<p_1$ to construct a physical inverse dephasing channel?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
It would require $q<0$, which is not a valid probability and does not define this CPTP channel. Recovery within a phase is state-dependent and uses information in neighboring degrees of freedom. It is not obtained by assigning negative noise to every edge or by inverting the channel on all possible input states.
:::
